p: (1) Save as otherwise provided by Parliament by law, every Union territory shall be administered by the President acting, to such extent as he thinks fit, through an administrator to be appointed by him with such designation as he may specify.

(2) Notwithstanding anything contained in Part VI, the President may appoint the Governor of a State as the administrator of an adjoining Union territory, and where a Governor is so appointed, he shall exercise his functions as such administrator independently of his Council of Ministers.]
f: Subs. by s. 17, ibid., for art. 239 (w.e.f. 1-11-1956).
239.s: Unless Parliament provides otherwise by law, the President runs every Union territory, acting as far as the President thinks fit through an administrator the President appoints. The President can make a neighbouring State's Governor the administrator, who then acts independently of the State's Council of Ministers.

p: (1) Parliament may by law create {2}[for the Union territory of {3}[Puducherry]]—
(a) a body, whether elected or partly nominated and partly elected, to function as a Legislature for the Union territory, or
(b) a Council of Ministers,
or both with such constitution, powers and functions, in each case, as may be specified in the law.

(2) Any such law as is referred to in clause (1) shall not be deemed to be an amendment of this Constitution for the purposes of article 368 notwithstanding that it contains any provision which amends or has the effect of amending this Constitution.]
f: Ins. by the Constitution (Fourteenth Amendment) Act, 1962, s. 4 (w.e.f. 28-12-1962).
Subs. by the Goa, Daman and Diu Reorganisation Act, 1987 (18 of 1987) s. 63, for "for any of the Union territories of Goa, Daman and Diu and Pondicherry" (w.e.f. 30-5-1987).
Subs. by the Pondicherry (Alteration of Name) Act, 2006 (44 of 2006), s. 4, for "Pondicherry" (w.e.f. 1-10-2006).
239A.s: Parliament can by law create for Puducherry an elected or partly nominated Legislature, a Council of Ministers, or both, with the powers it specifies. Such a law does not count as a constitutional amendment under Article 368, even if it changes the Constitution.

for any of the Union territories of Goa, Daman and Diu and Pondicherry

p: (1) As from the date of commencement of the Constitution (Sixty-ninth Amendment) Act, 1991, the Union territory of Delhi shall be called the National Capital Territory of Delhi (hereafter in this Part referred to as the National Capital Territory) and the administrator thereof appointed under article 239 shall be designated as the Lieutenant Governor.

(2)(a) There shall be a Legislative Assembly for the National Capital Territory and the seats in such Assembly shall be filled by members chosen by direct election from territorial constituencies in the National Capital Territory.

(b) The total number of seats in the Legislative Assembly, the number of seats reserved for Scheduled Castes, the division of the National Capital Territory into territorial constituencies (including the basis for such division) and all other matters relating to the functioning of the Legislative Assembly shall be regulated by law made by Parliament.
{2}[(ba) Seats shall be reserved for women in the Legislative Assembly of the National Capital Territory of Delhi.
(bb) As nearly as may be, one-third of the seats reserved for the Scheduled Castes in the Legislative Assembly of the National Capital Territory of Delhi shall be reserved for women.

(bc) As nearly as may be, one-third of the total number of seats to be filled by direct election in the Legislative Assembly of the National Capital Territory of Delhi (including the numbers of seats reserved for women belonging to the Scheduled Castes) shall be reserved for women in such manner as Parliament may by law determine.]

(c) The provisions of articles 324 to 327 and 329 shall apply in relation to the National Capital Territory, the Legislative Assembly of the National Capital Territory and the members thereof as they apply, in relation to a State, the Legislative Assembly of a State and the members thereof respectively; and any reference in articles 326 and 329 to “appropriate Legislature” shall be deemed to be a reference to Parliament.

(3) (a) Subject to the provisions of this Constitution, the Legislative Assembly shall have power to make laws for the whole or any part of the National Capital Territory with respect to any of the matters enumerated in the State List or in the Concurrent List in so far as any such matter is applicable to Union territories except matters with respect to Entries 1, 2 and 18 of the State List and Entries 64, 65 and 66 of that List in so far as they relate to the said Entries 1, 2 and 18.
(b) Nothing in sub-clause (a) shall derogate from the powers of Parliament under this Constitution to make laws with respect to any matter for a Union territory or any part thereof.

(c) If any provision of a law made by the Legislative Assembly with respect to any matter is repugnant to any provision of a law made by Parliament with respect to that matter, whether passed before or after the law made by the Legislative Assembly, or of an earlier law, other than a law made by the Legislative Assembly, then, in either case, the law made by Parliament, or, as the case may be, such earlier law, shall prevail and the law made by the Legislative Assembly shall, to the extent of the repugnancy, be void:

Provided that if any such law made by the Legislative Assembly has been reserved for the consideration of the President and has received his assent, such law shall prevail in the National Capital Territory:

Provided further that nothing in this sub-clause shall prevent Parliament from enacting at any time any law with respect to the same matter including a law adding to, amending, varying or repealing the law so made by the Legislative Assembly.

(4) There shall be a Council of Ministers consisting of not more than ten percent. of the total number of members in the Legislative Assembly, with the Chief Minister at the head to aid and advise the Lieutenant Governor in the exercise of his functions in relation to matters with respect to which the Legislative Assembly has power to make laws, except in so far as he is, by or under any law, required to act in his discretion:

Provided that in the case of difference of opinion between the Lieutenant Governor and his Ministers on any matter, the Lieutenant Governor shall refer it to the President for decision and act according to the decision given thereon by the President and pending such decision it shall be competent for the Lieutenant Governor in any case where the matter, in his opinion, is so urgent that it is necessary for him to take immediate action, to take such action or to give such direction in the matter as he deems necessary.

(5) The Chief Minister shall be appointed by the President and other Ministers shall be appointed by the President on the advice of the Chief Minister and the Ministers shall hold office during the pleasure of the President.
(6) The Council of Ministers shall be collectively responsible to the Legislative Assembly.
{3}[(7) (a)] Parliament may, by law, make provisions for giving effect to, or supplementing the provisions contained in the foregoing clauses and for all matters incidental or consequential thereto.

{4}[(b) Any such law as is referred to in sub-clause (a) shall not be deemed to be an amendment of this Constitution for the purposes of article 368 notwithstanding that it contains any provision which amends or has the effect of amending, this Constitution.]

(8) The provisions of article 239B shall, so far as may be, apply in relation to the National Capital Territory, the Lieutenant Governor and the Legislative Assembly, as they apply in relation to the Union territory of {5}[Puducherry], the administrator and its Legislature, respectively; and any reference in that article to “clause (1) of article 239A” shall be deemed to be a reference to this article or article 239AB, as the case may be.
f: Arts 239AA and 239 AB ins. by the Constitution (Sixty-ninth Amendment) Act, 1991, s. 2 (w.e.f. 1-2-1992).
Ins. by the Constitution (One-hundred and Sixth Amendment) Act, 2023, s. 2 (date yet (w.e.f. 16-4-2026).to be notified).
Subs. by the Constitution (Seventieth Amendment) Act, 1992, s. 3, for "(7)" (w.e.f. 21-12-1991).
Subs. by the Pondicherry (Alteration of Name) Act, 2006 (44 of 2006), s. 4, for "Pondicherry" (w.e.f. 1-10-2006). .
239AA.s: Delhi is the National Capital Territory, with an elected Legislative Assembly that can legislate on State and Concurrent List matters except State List Entries 1, 2 and 18 (public order, police and land). Seats are reserved for Scheduled Castes, and one-third will be reserved for women once the post-census delimitation under Article 334A happens. A Chief Minister-led Council of Ministers advises the Lieutenant Governor, who refers disagreements to the President, and Parliament's laws generally prevail over conflicting Assembly laws.

p: If the President, on receipt of a report from the Lieutenant Governor or otherwise, is satisfied—

(a) that a situation has arisen in which the administration of the National Capital Territory cannot be carried on in accordance with the provisions of article 239AA or of any law made in pursuance of that article; or
(b) that for the proper administration of the National Capital Territory it is necessary or expedient so to do,

the President may by order suspend the operation of any provision of article 239AA or of all or any of the provisions of any law made in pursuance of that article for such period and subject to such conditions as may be specified in such law and make such incidental and consequential provisions as may appear to him to be necessary or expedient for administering the National Capital Territory in accordance with the provisions of article 239 and article 239AA.]
239AB.s: If the President, on the Lieutenant Governor's report or otherwise, is satisfied that Delhi cannot be run under Article 239AA, or that it is needed for proper administration, the President can suspend any part of Article 239AA or laws made under it and make arrangements to run Delhi.

p: (1) If at any time, except when the Legislature of {2}[the Union territory of {3}[Puducherry]] is in session, the administrator thereof is satisfied that circumstances exist which render it necessary for him to take immediate action, he may promulgate such Ordinances as the circumstances appear to him to require:
Provided that no such Ordinance shall be promulgated by the administrator except after obtaining instructions from the President in that behalf:

Provided further that whenever the said Legislature is dissolved, or its functioning remains suspended on account of any action taken under any such law as is referred to in clause (1) of article 239A, the administrator shall not promulgate any Ordinance during the period of such dissolution or suspension.

(2) An Ordinance promulgated under this article in pursuance of instructions from the President shall be deemed to be an Act of the Legislature of the Union territory which has been duly enacted after complying with the provisions in that behalf contained in any such law as is referred to in clause (1) of article 239A, but every such Ordinance—

(a) shall be laid before the Legislature of the Union territory and shall cease to operate at the expiration of six weeks from the reassembly of the Legislature or if, before the expiration of that period, a resolution disapproving it is passed by the Legislature, upon the passing of the resolution; and
(b) may be withdrawn at any time by the administrator after obtaining instructions from the President in that behalf.

(3) If and so far as an Ordinance under this article makes any provision which would not be valid if enacted in an Act of the Legislature of the Union territory made after complying with the provisions in that behalf contained in any such law as is referred to in clause (1) of article 239A, it shall be void.]
f: Ins. by the Constitution (Twenty-seventh Amendment) Act, 1971, s. 3 (w.e.f. 30-12-1971).
Subs. by the Goa, Daman and Diu Reorganisation Act, 1987 (18 of 1987) s. 63, for "a Union territory referred to in clause (1) article 239A" (w.e.f. 30-5-1987).
Subs. by the Pondicherry (Alteration of Name) Act, 2006 (44 of 2006), s. 4, for "Pondicherry" (w.e.f. 1-10-2006).

Clause (4) ins. by the Constitution (Thirty-eighth Amendment) Act, 1975, s. 4 (with retrospective effect). This amendment was omitted by the Constitution (Forty-fourth Amendment) Act, 1978, s. 32 (w.e.f. 20-6-1979).
239B.s: When Puducherry's Legislature is not in session, its administrator can issue Ordinances for urgent action, but only on the President's instructions and never while the Legislature is dissolved or suspended. An Ordinance works like a law of the Legislature but lapses six weeks after the Legislature reassembles, or earlier if the Legislature disapproves it.

{10}[Provided further that whenever the body functioning as a Legislature for the Union territory of {11}[Puducherry] is dissolved, or the functioning of that body as such Legislature remains suspended on account of any action taken under any such law as is referred to in clause (1) of article 239A, the President may, during the period of such dissolution or suspension, make regulations for the peace, progress and good government of that Union territory.]

(2) Any regulation so made may repeal or amend any Act made by Parliament or {12}[any other law], which is for the time being applicable to the Union territory and, when promulgated by the President, shall have the same force and effect as an Act of Parliament which applies to that territory.]

For Puducherry, this power stops once its Legislature first meets, except while it is dissolved or suspended.

p: (1) Parliament may by law constitute a High Court for a {1}[Union territory] or declare any court in any {2}[such territory] to be a High Court for all or any of the purposes of this Constitution.

(2) The provisions of Chapter V of Part VI shall apply in relation to every High Court referred to in clause (1) as they apply in relation to a High Court referred to in article 214 subject to such modifications or exceptions as Parliament may by law provide.

{3}[(3) Subject to the provisions of this Constitution and to the provisions of any law of the appropriate Legislature made by virtue of powers conferred on that Legislature by or under this Constitution, every High Court exercising jurisdiction immediately before the commencement of the Constitution (Seventh Amendment) Act, 1956, in relation to any Union territory shall continue to exercise such jurisdiction in relation to that territory after such commencement.
(4) Nothing in this article derogates from the power of Parliament to extend or exclude the jurisdiction of a High Court for a State to, or from, any Union territory or part thereof.]
f: Subs. by the Constitution (Seventh Amendment) Act, 1956, s. 29 and Sch., for "State specified in Part C of the First Schedule" (w.e.f. 1-11-1956).
Subs. by s. 29. and Sch., ibid., for "such State" (w.e.f. 1-11-1956).
Subs. by s. 29, and Sch., ibid., for cls. (3) and (4) (w.e.f. 1-11-1956).
241.s: Parliament can by law create a High Court for a Union territory or declare a court there to be a High Court, and the rules for State High Courts apply with any changes Parliament makes. High Courts already covering a Union territory before 1956 continue to do so.
fh: State specified in Part C of the First Schedule

242.st: Omitted by the Constitution (Seventh Amendment) Act, 1956, s. 29 and Sch.(w.e.f. 1-11-1956).

why: Minerva Mills (1980) held that abrogating Articles 14 and 19 for a class of laws destroys the basic structure; Coelho (2007) treats the essence of Articles 14, 19 and 21 as the test for Ninth Schedule laws.
Coelho (2007) called Article 32 "an important and integral part of the basic structure", and L. Chandra Kumar (1997) held that judicial review under it cannot be ousted.
L. Chandra Kumar (1997) held that the High Courts' power of judicial review under Article 226, and their superintendence under Article 227, are part of the inviolable basic structure.
Minerva Mills (1980) held that a limited amending power is itself a basic feature, so Parliament cannot amend this article to make its power unlimited.

The NJAC case (2015) struck down the Ninety-ninth Amendment's new method of appointing judges as a breach of judicial independence, so the core of how judges are appointed is part of the basic structure.
Names India as a Union of States. Abolishing the Union or the States would undo federalism and India's sovereignty, both part of the framework.
This is the hook for testing laws against fundamental rights. Courts have said the power to test legislation "can never be ousted".
Core guarantees against discrimination and untouchability. Coelho (2007) named Article 15 among the rights forming part of the basic structure.
Freedom of religion is the main textual home of secularism, which the Court has repeatedly called a basic feature.
Judicial review by the High Courts, held to be basic, depends on the High Courts existing.
Adult suffrage is the foundation of democracy and free and fair elections.
Kesavananda Bharati (Khanna J) held that the part of the Preamble relating to the basic structure cannot be amended; Balram Singh (2024) upheld adding "socialist" and "secular".
Defines "the State" against which fundamental rights are enforced; gutting it would hollow out the rights.
Equality of opportunity in public employment is part of the equality code, though clauses on reservation have been changed and upheld.
Basic protections of personal liberty and fair criminal process, closely tied to Article 21.
Bans on forced labour and child labour in hazardous work relate to human dignity; no case has tested their repeal.
Religious freedom of groups and the bar on State religious instruction carry secularism into practice.
Minority rights to culture and to run educational institutions support pluralism and secularism.
The Directive to separate the judiciary from the executive expresses separation of powers and judicial independence.
An elected President as head of state is part of the republican form of government.
How the President is elected. Entrenched: changing it needs ratification by half the States.
Extent of Union executive power, one half of the federal balance. Entrenched under Article 368(2).
Ministers advise the President and answer collectively to the Lok Sabha: the core of parliamentary government.
An elected Parliament, with the States represented in it. Representation of the States is entrenched.
Fixed terms for the Houses guarantee periodic elections.
Parliament cannot discuss a judge's conduct except on a motion for removal, a rule tied to judicial independence.
Judges' salaries cannot be cut to their disadvantage while in office, a guard on judicial independence.
Courts of record with power to punish contempt, part of the courts' ability to make their orders effective.
The Supreme Court settles disputes between the Union and the States, a federal safeguard.
Special leave to appeal lets the Supreme Court correct any court or tribunal, central to access to justice.
Each State has its own executive, part of the federal structure.
Extent of State executive power. Entrenched under Article 368(2).
State ministers advise the Governor and answer to the Assembly: parliamentary government at State level.
An elected State Legislature with fixed terms, needed for both democracy and federalism.
Transfers of High Court judges. The NJAC case struck down the 2014 change to this article as part of the same scheme.
High Court control over the subordinate courts keeps the district judiciary independent of the executive.
The division of law-making power between Parliament and the States. Entrenched under Article 368(2).
No tax without the authority of law, a basic rule-of-law guarantee.
An independent Election Commission conducts elections; without it free and fair elections would be at risk.
A single electoral roll with no exclusion on grounds of religion, race, caste or sex.
The right to education. Its insertion was upheld, but no case says whether removing it would breach the basic structure.
The welfare-state directives most closely tied to the balance between Parts III and IV. Removing them might upset that balance; untested.
Courts cannot question the validity of legislative proceedings on grounds of procedure. Touches both separation of powers and judicial review.
Binding precedent and the power to do complete justice. Important to the Court's role, but not tested as basic.
An independent auditor of public accounts supports the rule of law and accountability; untested.
Organisational rules for the High Courts. Some core is needed for judicial review, but the details can change.
President's Rule. Its use is reviewable (Bommai), and abuse can damage federalism and democracy, but the article itself is not part of the basic structure.
Suspension of rights during emergency. Since 1978, Articles 20 and 21 cannot be suspended; widening this power again could touch the essence of rights.
Parliament already changes State boundaries by ordinary law; the federal structure survives individual changes.
Citizenship rules. Parliament already controls citizenship by law under Article 11.
These shield certain laws from fundamental rights challenges. Removing them would restore rights, not damage the structure.
Powers to adapt or restrict rights for armed forces and martial law; administrative in nature.
Individual Directive Principles. The balance between Parts III and IV is basic, but no single directive has been held essential.
Fundamental duties were added in 1976 and are not enforceable in court.
Detailed rules on the President, Vice-President and conduct of business. Can change without touching a basic feature.
Detailed rules on Parliament's membership, officers and procedure.
Legislative and financial procedure, and ordinances. Can be redesigned without damaging democracy itself.
Organisation and jurisdiction of the Supreme Court beyond its core review power. Many have been amended before.
Form and reporting of public accounts.
Detailed rules on Governors and State executive business.
Detailed rules on State Legislatures, their officers and members.
State legislative and financial procedure, assent to Bills and ordinances.
Detailed rules on High Court judges and jurisdiction beyond the core review power.
Appointment and rules for district judges and subordinate courts.
How Union territories are governed. Parliament has changed this often.
Panchayats, added in 1992. Local democracy, but not part of the original framework or any holding.
Administration of Scheduled and Tribal Areas.
Specific rules within the division of legislative power. Entrenched where in Chapter I of Part XI, but individually changeable.
Administrative relations between the Union and the States.
Distribution of revenues and the Finance Commission. Revised many times, including by GST in 2016.
Freedom of trade within India and its exceptions.
Civil services and Public Service Commissions.
Tribunals may exist; what is part of the basic structure is the High Courts' and Supreme Court's review over them, not these articles.
Election law-making and the bar on courts during elections.
Reservations in legislatures and services, commissions and lists. Many have sunset clauses or have been amended; upheld when changed.
Linguistic minority protections and the Hindi directive.
Emergency powers. The articles themselves are not part of the basic structure.
Transitional provisions continuing earlier laws, courts and officers.
The right to property. Kesavananda Bharati (Khanna J) held it is not part of the basic structure.
Temporary and special provisions for particular States. Several have been changed or abrogated and upheld.
Abolition of titles. An equality measure, but minor; no case suggests it is essential.
Equal justice and free legal aid, the directive most closely tied to effective access to justice.
Concurrent power over GST, added in 2016. A specific fiscal arrangement within federalism.
Interpretation clause for the Part on finance.
Co-operative societies, added in 2011. Detailed regulatory rules.
Salaries of members and rules of procedure and language in Parliament.
Definitions, interpretation, short title, commencement, the Hindi text and repeals.
Lists the States and Union territories. Parliament changes it by ordinary law under Articles 3 and 4.
Salaries and allowances of constitutional office-holders.
Forms of oaths, including the oath to uphold the Constitution.
Allocation of Rajya Sabha seats. Entrenched, but the numbers change by amendment.
Autonomous districts in the North-East; amended many times.
The Union, State and Concurrent Lists as a scheme are the core of federalism. Individual entries are changed often.
Laws shielded from fundamental rights challenges. Removing the shield would not damage the structure.
The anti-defection law, upheld in Kihoto Hollohan. Repealing it would not breach a basic feature.

amend.s: Parliament can amend any part of the Constitution, but cannot use that power to destroy its identity or make the power unlimited.

jr.s: The High Courts and the Supreme Court must be able to test laws and government action against the Constitution.

indep.s: Judges must be appointed and kept in office free of control by the executive.

rol.c: P. Sambamurthy (1986); I.R. Coelho (2007); Raj Narain (1975)
rol.s: Government acts under law, and its decisions can be tested by independent courts.

equality.t: Equality and the essence of fundamental rights
equality.s: The core of Articles 14, 19 and 21, and the essence of each fundamental right, cannot be abrogated.

balance.t: Balance between Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles
balance.s: Parts III and IV must be kept in harmony; neither may be made to swallow the other.

democracy.c: Kesavananda Bharati (1973, Sikri CJ); S.R. Bommai (1994)
democracy.s: Government by elected representatives, with an elected head of state.

elections.s: Elections must be free and fair, and their results open to lawful challenge.

secular.c: S.R. Bommai (1994); I.R. Coelho (2007); Balram Singh (2024)
secular.s: The State treats all religions equally and has no religion of its own.

federal.c: Kesavananda Bharati (1973, Sikri CJ); S.R. Bommai (1994)
federal.s: Power is divided between the Union and the States, and the States are not mere agents of the Centre.

sop.c: Kesavananda Bharati (1973, Sikri CJ); I.R. Coelho (2007); Presidential Reference on assent to Bills (2025)
sop.s: Legislature, executive and judiciary each keep their own sphere.

supremacy.s: Every organ of the State is bound by the Constitution.

sovereign.c: Listed by the Lok Sabha Secretariat (2008)
sovereign.s: India is a sovereign Union; its unity and integrity are part of the framework.

parl.c: Listed by the Lok Sabha Secretariat (2008)
parl.s: Ministers are drawn from and answerable to an elected legislature.

access.c: Listed by the Lok Sabha Secretariat (2008)
access.s: People must be able to reach a court to enforce their rights.
